newsitem.title: USA: Obesity linked to viruses in some.
newsitem.headline: Obesity linked to viruses in some.

text.p: Some obese people may have been infected with a family of viruses that experiments have shown cause similar gross weight gain in laboratory animals, researchers said on Monday.

Comparing the alarming worldwide increase in obesity to an epidemic disease, University of Wisconsin Medical School researchers found the blood of 15 percent of 154 obese people tested had antibodies to the adenovirus named Ad-36.

None of the 45 lean volunteers in the study had signs of the virus, one of a group of 50 viruses that typically are transmitted through the air and can cause upper respiratory infections, cold symptoms, gastrointestinal problems and eye inflammation.

The study, conducted by assistant research scientist Nikhil Dhurandhar and professor of medicine and nutritional sciences Richard Atkinson, was presented on Monday at the Experimental Biology annual meeting in New Orleans.

In his earlier work, Dhurandhar said he found that one type of adenovirus found only in his native India infects birds and could induce obesity when injected into chickens. He repeated the experiments on other laboratory animals with similar results.
"A paradoxical characteristic of the virus is that in animals it appears to produce low levels of cholesterol and triglycerides along with the obesity," Dhurandhar said.

Cholesterol and triglycerides, fatty substances which can block arteries and cause heart disease, were also found to be at low levels in the bloodstreams of obese people who had the antibodies. Obese people who did not have signs of ever being infected had the expected elevated levels of fatty substances.
Among men, the study found that the presence of the antibodies was associated with a significantly better response to treatment with obesity drugs.

Atkinson said there had been an "alarming" worldwide increase in obesity in the past 30 years, and that obesity rates in the United States had climbed 30 percent from 1980 to 1990. Between 80 million to 90 million Americans were obese, defined as a body-mass index of 27 or above based on dividing a person's weight in kilograms by the square of height in meters.
"This increase is the type of pattern that might occur with a new infectious disease," Atkinson noted.
More research was needed to determine if increasing rates of obesity cold be attributed to infection with Ad-36, the researchers said.
